title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text:
In class we built a house price model for Philadelphia. Now your team does it for a city you haven’t modeled: Chicago.
The Cook County Assessor’s Office has to value every home in the county, including the vast majority that didn’t sell this year. Assessments drive property tax bills. When they’re wrong in a systematic way, some households pay more than their share. A 2017 Chicago Tribune investigation, “The Tax Divide,” found exactly that in Cook County: lower-value homes were assessed at higher shares of their worth than expensive ones.
Build a model that predicts single-family sale prices in Chicago, 2023–2025, using only the tools from this course. The file contains only features of the house itself. Everything about location is yours to build.









File
What’s in it




chicago_train.csv
About 80% of the houses, with sale prices


chicago_test.csv
The other 20%, without sale prices. You predict them; we score you.



The test houses were held out by house, not by sale, so a house that sold twice is entirely on one side. Your CV RMSE is your estimate. Your test RMSE is the truth. If they’re far apart, something leaked.
Due: Friday, October 30. All teammates renders the file on their portfolio and every member submits that link on Canvas. One teammate uploads team_XX_predictions.csv.
Individual accountability: Q7 on October 30 asks each of you about this model: which features you used and why, your CV and test RMSE, and where the model fails worst. Make sure everyone can explain all of it.









Important1. Clean training rows once, in Part 1. Never drop test rows.



You must predict every test house, so fill NAs in a feature rather than filtering.


Open data from 2023–2025 only.



Nothing built from sale prices. Would the Assessor have this number for a house that didn’t sell?



Transform predictors, not sale_price.



No features built from other houses’ sale prices.













Model log
Every model you tried, in order, with CV RMSE and Moran’s I. Each row has a note saying why you tried it.


Features
Incorporate the feature engineering tricks - including the spatial ones covered these past few weeks.


Diagnostics
Residual maps for your baseline and final model, and what changed.


Error analysis
Where your final model fails worst, and whose homes it over-values (Part 4).

Choices justified by evidence from your own analysis.

check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}

moran_cv <- function(formula, train, k = 8) {
  model <- lm(formula, data = st_drop_geometry(train))
  residuals <- residuals(model)
  coords <- st_coordinates(
    st_point_on_surface(train)
  )
  neighbors <- spdep::knearneigh(
    coords,
    k = k,
    longlat = FALSE
  )
  neighbors_list <- spdep::knn2nb(neighbors)

  weights <- spdep::nb2listw(
    neighbors_list,
    style = "W",
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  result <- spdep::moran.test(
    residuals,
    weights,
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  as.numeric(result$estimate[["Moran I statistic"]])
}

w_knn <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(map_residuals_final), k = 5)), style = "W")
lisa_quads <- function(resid, w, alpha = 0.01) {
  lm_perm <- localmoran_perm(resid, w, nsim = 499)
  z   <- resid - mean(resid)
  lag <- lag.listw(w, z)
  p   <- lm_perm[, "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"]
  case_when(
    p >= alpha        ~ "Not significant",
    z > 0 & lag > 0   ~ "High-High",
    z < 0 & lag < 0   ~ "Low-Low",
    z > 0 & lag < 0   ~ "High-Low",
    TRUE              ~ "Low-High"
  )
}

Why the model under-predicts in the red cluster?
The red cluster is along the North Side lakefront in Lincoln Park and Lakeview, and here our model guesses too low. We think this is because our features can measure how far a home is from a park, school or train station, but not how special that place is. Living near the lake, right next to Lincoln Park, or inside the Lincoln or Blaine school boundaries adds a lot to a home’s price, and the model has no way to see that. A lot of homes here have been fully renovated or rebuilt, but our data only has the original build year, so the model treats a brand-new interior like a 120-year-old house.
Why the model over-predicts in Beverly and the other blue clusters?
Our model guesses too high in Beverly, and we think it’s because Beverly looks like a rich North Side neighborhood to our model. The model doesn’t account for how far it is from downtown. It has high incomes, lots of college graduates, high homeownership and few vacant homes. In Chicago, most neighborhoods like that are close to the Loop, so when the model learned that higher income means higher prices, part of that was really about being central. Beverly is wealthy but about 15 miles from downtown, so the model gives it a boost it doesn’t earn. Beverly also has two landmark districts and several Metra stops, and the model learned those as price boosts mostly from places like Lincoln Park and Old Town, which are much closer to the downtown. On top of that, a few very large historic homes on the ridge pull up the neighborhood averages, so the regular bungalows nearby get predicted higher than they actually sell for. We see a similar pattern in the blue clusters on the far Northwest Side, around Edison Park and Norwood Park. These are also comfortable neighborhoods far from downtown, so the model reads the good demographics and misses the distance.

Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

Read one coefficient twice: once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.

The coefficient of building_000sf (each home’s square footage) is 382,377. This means that when holding all other variables constant, an increase of 1,000 sq feet is associated with a 382,377 higher sale price based on the training data. Its standard error is 4,961, which tells us how much the coefficient may vary if we had a different sample.
When the model predicts on the test data, it adds $382,377 per 1,000 sq ft (or 382 dollars per 1 sq ft) to every house in every neighborhood. As we noted earlier, the model applies this average to every house, no matter the neighborhood. The issue here is that relationships change across space (spacial non-stationarity), so an additional 500 sq is worth more in areas with more expensive land. This appears to be one reason why we get clustered errors.

Would you hand this model to the Assessor? What would you warn them about?

We would not hand this model to the Assessor yet because our residual map still shows some spatial clustering. While it is not egregious (Moran’s I is .23 for final model), it does mean that our model is missing a spatial variable that would more accurately predict the sales prices. Ultimately, this means that the model could more accurately predict sales prices. We would warn them that our model underpredicts the red clustered points in North Side lakefront in Lincoln Park and Lakeview and that it overpredicts the blue clustered points in Beverly.
We would also tell the assessor that we did relatively light data manipulation ahead of our regression analysis. We kept all homes in our data that sold for more than $1. There were 108 houses that sold for less than $25,000. This means that our data presumably included figures that were non market sales. text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at median home value across counties in Maryland, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably. As someone house-hunting in the Baltimore, I wanted to know how reliable home value estimates really are before treating them as fact. This matters beyond my own search as well since, shaky estimates affect property tax assessments and lending decisions too, so it’s useful for anyone relying on this data, not just buyers.

Is the margin of error bigger in small places?

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

This matches what I expected: the ACS samples fewer households in smaller counties, so their estimates carry more uncertainty. Simply put, the most populated counties have the smallest margin of error and thus the highest confidence, and vice-versa

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The Maryland counties we know least about, statistically speaking, are Kent, Somerset, Garrett, and Dorchester. Each shows the highest moe_pct in the dataset, meaning their median home value estimates carry the largest margin of error relative to the estimate itself. This isn’t a coincidence: these are also the state’s least populated counties, and since the ACS is a sample survey, smaller counties yield smaller samples, which produces less statistically reliable estimates. Large, densely populated counties like Montgomery, Prince George’s, and Baltimore City, by contrast, are surveyed far more heavily and show much smaller margins of error.
If a state agency used median home value to allocate funding, for example, directing more support toward counties with lower home values and treated every county’s number as equally certain; the small, low-reliability counties would bear all the risk. If a county like Somerset’s true home value is actually higher than its shaky estimate suggests, it risks receiving too little funding relative to its real need. If the true value is actually lower, it risks receiving more than it needs, pulling funding away from counties that could use it more. Meanwhile, large counties like Montgomery are essentially unaffected by this risk, since their estimates are already precise. In short, the places we measure least reliably are exactly the places most likely to be misjudged when that data drives real decisions.

The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}

text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))

Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?

  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))

A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)

Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = jobs_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(jobs_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()











Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = pop_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(pop_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)

Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:

  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal()











5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 3 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 8 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").






NoteCheck your group sizes



If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.

Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer: Distance to City Hall helped the most. Once I let it curve (distance plus distance squared), CV RMSE dropped from 5.15 to 5.02. The scatterplot made sense of it: commutes get longer as you move away from the center, peak around 8 to 9 miles out, then ease off. A straight line can’t do that.
Job density was the big letdown. I expected it to matter, but it actually made predictions worse (5.20), and logging it only got me back to 5.12. I think that’s because jobs show where people work, while my outcome is how long residents take to get there. It also moves a lot with population density, so it didn’t add much new.
For one coefficient, take the share of adults with a bachelor’s degree. Holding everything else constant, each extra percentage point of college graduates goes with a commute about 0.05 minutes shorter. Two similar tracts that are 10 points apart in college share are predicted to differ by about 0.47 minutes, or about 28 seconds, with the more educated tract having the shorter commute.
My final residual map still has a few stubborn spots: one dark red tract in the north-center, and some dark blue ones in the center-right and south. I’d want to know how good the bus service and highway access are there. SEPTA’s schedule data (GTFS, from 2023 or earlier) could show bus frequency, and OpenStreetMap or Census road files could show highway access.
As for noise, the fog plot shows that tracts with shakier commute estimates tend to be missed by more, around 3 minutes at the low end and 9 at the high end. But plenty of reliable tracts are still missed by a lot, so uncertainty explains part of the error, not most of it.
